d: The part of the prostate that surrounds the urethra just below the bladder. It is the zone that develops benign prostatic hyperplasia, so its overgrowth squeezes the urethra early and causes urinary symptoms.
The back and side part of the prostate, about 70% of the gland. It lies against the rectum, so a hard nodule can be felt on rectal exam, and about 70 to 80% of prostate cancers begin here.

A strong androgen made from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase in the prostate and genital skin. It binds the androgen receptor more tightly than testosterone does and drives prostate growth, so BPH needs it.

Prostate-specific antigen, a protease made by prostate cells that thins semen. It is organ-specific, not cancer-specific: BPH, prostatitis, instrumentation and ejaculation raise it, and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors halve it.

The flat layer of cells under the secretory cells of normal prostate glands, shown by p63 and high-molecular-weight keratin stains. Its absence in small crowded glands is the key sign of prostate adenocarcinoma.

The tough, inelastic fibrous sheath around the corpora cavernosa. It traps blood during an erection, scars into a plaque in Peyronie disease, and can rupture in penile fracture when the erect penis is bent.
Planned monitoring of low-risk prostate cancer with repeated PSA tests, MRI and biopsy, with treatment only if the cancer progresses. It answers the problem of overdiagnosing latent disease.
